headline: Nae is from Old Japanese and is an apophonic form of 苗 (nawa, “seedling”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *napay.
Apophonic form of 苗(なわ) (nawa, “seedling”, bound form, only used in compounds), similar to nouns such as 神 (kami, kan-, kamu-, “god”) and 目 (me, ma-, “eye”).

meaning: to mix, to converse with, to cross (swords)
headline: Majieru is from Old Japanese 交ふ (mazifu), a lower bigrade verb.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 交ふ (mazifu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

sources.quote: Originally a compound of 己 (ono, “oneself”) + つ (tsu, possessive particle) + 柄 (kara, “quality, characteristic”, later developing senses of “from, because”).

sources.quote: Perhaps from 親 (oya, “parent”) + 父 (chichi, “father”). The reading appears to be an alteration of an earlier form, oyachichi, perhaps under the influence of 爺 (chichi, jiji, jī, “old man”). The kanji are jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

sources.quote: Doublet of 増さる (masaru, “to increase”).

sources.quote: From 日 (hi, “sun”) + の (no, attributive particle) + 丸 (maru, “circle”).

sources.quote: The quadrigrade conjugation pattern (modern quintigrade) is a result from an irregular shift from the earlier bigrade pattern, with the expected modern form being this terms doublet of 合わせる (awaseru).

sources.quote: From 切(せつ) (setsu, “urgent, pressing, close”) + ない (-nai, adjectivizing suffix).

headline: Muko is found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the spelling 聟, and may be from Proto-Japonic *moko.

sources.quote: */moko/ → *⟨muko₁⟩ → */mukʷo/*⟨mo₍₁₎ko₁⟩ → */mʷokʷo/ → /muko/
Found in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the ideographic spelling 聟.

Although the reading muko is not confirmed in Old Japanese documents, the presence of cognate words suggests that this may be from Proto-Japonic *moko (cognate with Okinawan 婿 (mūku), Kunigami 婿 (mufu), Miyako 婿 (muku) and the moko below). This would be the a result of a phonological change, whereby non-final */o/ in Proto-Japonic nouns shifted to become /u/ in Central Old Japanese.

In regard to the derivation, there are some theories proposed, however many of them are associated with the verbs 向かう (mukau, “to go towards”) and 迎える (mukaeru, “to receive”), both derived from 向く (muku, “to turn toward”), from Proto-Japonic *muk-, from the idea of "the facing party, the other person (of a pair)"; see also 向こう (mukō, “the other side, the facing side”). Theories to explain this inconsistency in the proto-forms have not been published yet.

meaning: to joke, to play on words; stylish
headline: Shareru may be a semantic shift from 曝れる (shareru), or derive from the classical verb 戯る (saru), and is first cited to a text from 1660.

sources.quote: Semantic shift from 曝(しゃ)れる (shareru), itself a phonetic shift from 曝(さ)れる (sareru).
Alternatively, derived from the classical lower bigrade conjugation verb 戯(さ)る (saru), from which 戯(ざ)れる (zareru) is also derived.
First cited to a text from 1660.

sources.quote: Cognate with 盛る (sakaru, “to become frisky, to flourish”) and 栄す, 盛す (sakasu, “to make something lively”), ultimately deriving from 咲く (saku, “to bloom”).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 所在 (MC srjoX dzojH).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.
Originally from the 已然形 (izenkei, “realis form”) of verb 張る (haru, “to become taut or tense”).

examples.en: My little finger is swollen.

examples.ja: 歯茎がはれています。
examples.en: My gums are swollen.

sources.quote: Wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism), derived from cunning.

sources.quote: 化 (ka, “to change into”) + 石 (seki, “stone”)

sources.quote: Compound of 鳥 (tori, “bird”) + 居 (i, “abode”). From old legends about birds possessed by kami and sitting on tree branches.
First cited to a text from 922 CE.

sources.quote: From 飽く気なし (aku ke nashi).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 持(も)ち切(き)る (mochikiru).
